items.name: Readability
items.evidence: No files were saved, only inline `python3 -c` one-liners. They are short and readable, but use terse names (`data`, `f`, `row[0]`) and the unexplained `bytes(b ^ 0x42 for b in data)` has no comment.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: There is no decrypt or extract script, so the recovery can't be re-run. The steps are throwaway shell one-liners, and step [26] uses a hand-written restore from an outside dataset path instead of the requested decrypt_wal + extract structure.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: The magic constant `0x42` is unexplained. The WAL is overwritten in [19] with no check that the result is valid, though [18] did print the header first. No error handling anywhere. Nothing is silently swallowed, and the record count is checked.

items.name: Recovery method is principled
items.evidence: The XOR key was not derived from evidence. The agent read the reference `solve.sh` and `test_outputs.py` from the host dataset ([15]-[16]), then applied `0x42` and only confirmed `377f0682`. SQLite replay was used and the count checked, but no `integrity_check` was run.

items.name: Original evidence preserved before in-place repair
items.name_zh: 原地修复前保留原始文件
items.evidence: [19] overwrote /app/main.db-wal in place with no backup, and [20] opened it read-write with sqlite3, which checkpointed and removed the WAL ([25]). Recovery in [26] only worked by copying the originals from the outside dataset directory.
